beats.title: Confucius's Analects
beats.description: Sayings and conversations of a teacher of ethics, duty and good government were gathered by his followers after his death.
beats.note: Year of his death, used as the traditional anchor; the text was compiled later.

beats.title: Socrates on Trial
beats.description: An Athenian jury convicted the questioning philosopher of impiety and corrupting the young, and he drank hemlock.

beats.title: Plato's Republic
beats.description: A dialogue imagines the perfect city ruled by philosophers and asks what justice really is.

beats.title: Aristotle Opens the Lyceum
beats.description: Back in Athens, Plato's former pupil founded his own school and taught logic, ethics and the natural world while walking.

beats.title: Epicurus Founds the Garden
beats.description: A philosopher began teaching in a garden school that held the goal of life to be calm pleasure and freedom from fear.

beats.title: Zeno Teaches Stoicism
beats.description: A shipwrecked merchant began lecturing beneath a painted porch in Athens on living by reason and accepting fate.
beats.why_in: founding teaching of Stoicism by Zeno
beats.note: Approximate; sources agree only on about 300 BCE, and 301 keeps the years distinct.

beats.title: Laozi's Tao Te Ching
beats.description: A short book of sayings on the Way, simplicity and effortless action became the root text of Taoist thought in China.
beats.note: Scholars place composition in the late 4th century BCE; the excavated Guodian text predates 300 BCE. The 6th-century date is traditional.

beats.title: Lucretius's On the Nature of Things
beats.description: A Roman poet set out the atomic philosophy of Epicurus in a long verse poem urging readers not to fear death.
beats.note: Approximate; 55 BCE is his traditional death date, the poem was circulating by early 54 BCE, and proposed death years run from 55 to 49 BCE.

beats.title: Nagarjuna's Middle Way Verses
beats.description: An Indian Buddhist philosopher argued in verse that all things lack fixed essence, founding the Madhyamaka school.
beats.note: Approximate; scholars date him to the 2nd century CE.

beats.title: Marcus Aurelius's Meditations
beats.description: A Roman emperor wrote private notes to himself on duty, impermanence and Stoic calm while campaigning on the frontier.
beats.note: Written in his last years, traditionally dated to his death.

beats.title: Augustine's Confessions
beats.description: A North African bishop wrote a searching spiritual autobiography that shaped Western ideas of the self, will and time.

beats.title: Boethius's Consolation
beats.description: A Roman statesman awaiting execution wrote a dialogue with Lady Philosophy on fortune, happiness and fate.

beats.title: Avicenna's Book of Healing
beats.description: A Persian polymath completed a vast encyclopedia of logic, natural science and metaphysics that shaped thought in East and West.

beats.title: Al-Ghazali's Incoherence
beats.description: A Baghdad scholar attacked the Greek-inspired reasoning of earlier Muslim thinkers and reshaped Islamic philosophy.

beats.title: Maimonides Writes His Guide
beats.description: A Jewish scholar in Cairo wrote a work reconciling Aristotelian reason with scripture for readers troubled by doubt.

beats.title: Aquinas Begins the Summa Theologiae
beats.description: A Dominican friar started his vast synthesis of Aristotle and Christian doctrine, including his five arguments for God.

beats.title: Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah
beats.description: A North African scholar wrote an introduction to history that analysed the rise and fall of dynasties and societies.

beats.title: Wang Yangming's Enlightenment
beats.description: Exiled to a remote post, a Chinese official realised that moral knowledge lies in the mind itself, founding a new school.

beats.title: Machiavelli's The Prince
beats.description: A Florentine diplomat's blunt handbook on gaining and holding power was printed, shocking readers with its cold realism.

beats.title: Montaigne's Essays
beats.description: A French nobleman retired to his tower and published a book of personal, questioning reflections that created a new literary form.

beats.title: Bacon's Novum Organum
beats.description: An English statesman set out a new method of learning by observation and induction to replace medieval reasoning.

beats.title: Descartes: I Think, Therefore I Am
beats.description: A French thinker doubted everything and found one certainty, launching modern philosophy in his Discourse on Method.

beats.title: Hobbes's Leviathan
beats.description: An English philosopher argued that people need a powerful sovereign to escape a life that is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.

beats.title: Spinoza's Ethics
beats.description: A Dutch lens grinder's geometric treatise identified God with nature and was published only after his death.

beats.title: Locke's Essay on Understanding
beats.description: An English philosopher argued that the mind begins as a blank slate and all knowledge comes from experience.

beats.title: Hume's A Treatise of Human Nature
beats.description: A young Scottish thinker tried to build a science of the mind and questioned cause, the self and reason.

beats.title: Rousseau's The Social Contract
beats.description: A Genevan thinker opened with the claim that man is born free yet everywhere in chains, and grounded rule in the general will.

beats.title: Kant's Critique of Pure Reason
beats.description: A Prussian professor argued that the mind shapes the experience it receives, reshaping the limits of human knowledge.

beats.title: Bentham's Principles of Morals
beats.description: An English reformer set out the idea that the right act is the one producing the greatest happiness for the greatest number.

beats.title: Wollstonecraft's Vindication
beats.description: A London writer argued that women are not naturally inferior to men and only appear so for lack of education.

beats.title: Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit
beats.description: A German philosopher traced consciousness through stages of struggle toward absolute knowledge, popularising dialectical thinking.

beats.title: Schopenhauer's World as Will
beats.description: A gloomy German thinker claimed that blind striving underlies all reality and that art and compassion offer relief.

beats.title: Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling
beats.description: A Danish writer used the story of Abraham and Isaac to probe faith, anxiety and the leap beyond reason.

beats.title: The Communist Manifesto
beats.description: Two German thinkers declared that history is a story of class struggle and called on workers of the world to unite.
beats.why_in: defining work of Marx and Engels

beats.title: Mill's On Liberty
beats.description: An English philosopher defended free speech and individual freedom, limited only by harm to others.
beats.why_in: defining work of J. S. Mill

beats.title: Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra
beats.description: A German philosopher announced that God is dead and imagined the Overman who creates new values.

beats.title: Gandhi's Hind Swaraj
beats.description: Written aboard a ship in under two weeks, a short book set out a vision of self-rule through nonviolence.

beats.title: Wittgenstein's Tractatus
beats.description: A short, numbered book claimed that the limits of language are the limits of the world and that much philosophy is nonsense.

beats.title: Heidegger's Being and Time
beats.description: A German philosopher revived the question of what it means to be, analysing human existence in the world.

beats.title: Sartre's Being and Nothingness
beats.description: A French writer argued that existence precedes essence and that humans are condemned to be free.

beats.title: Beauvoir's The Second Sex
beats.description: A French philosopher argued that one is not born but becomes a woman, founding modern feminist theory.

beats.title: Rawls's A Theory of Justice
beats.description: A Harvard philosopher proposed choosing society's rules from behind a veil of ignorance about one's own place in it.
